questions: Go through every project won in the last 12 to 24 months in your CRM or invoices and note for each how the client first found you (referral, walk-in, in-person pitch, event, website, repeat client); what share depended on meeting in person or on the office location?

Ask your two or three largest clients directly, with a concrete question: would you still run workshops and sign-offs with us by video only, and would you consider moving work to an agency with its own premises?
Ask each team member privately (not in a group survey): would you want to work fully remote five days a week, and what does your home workspace look like? Include juniors and quieter members.

Run a trial of one to two months with no one in the office on the usual shared days: what happens to review turnaround, the number of rework rounds and client feedback compared with the two previous months?

How do your junior designers currently get feedback and learn: write down how many hours per week they spend sitting with seniors, and decide what concrete replacement (scheduled pairing, review sessions) would cover it remotely.
Have an accountant or payroll advisor check where each employee lives and works and which payroll, insurance, equipment and tax obligations fully remote work would trigger; what is the yearly cost?

Add up the costs the quarter-saving figure leaves out: home-office stipends, co-working or meeting room bookings for client workshops, software, equipment shipping and insurance; what is the net saving after them?

Ask the landlord whether a shorter lease, a smaller space, or a break clause is available, and check what comparable offices in the area would cost and how fast they are available if you needed to return.

Look at your last three hires or candidate pipelines: how many asked about the office, and how would you onboard a junior remotely? Ask two recruiters or peer studios what remote candidates in your field expect.
Can you test a cheaper middle option, such as a smaller office or a co-working desk package with a meeting room for four weeks, to see how client meetings and walk-in leads change?

lean.option: Give up the office and go remote
lean.reasons: Fixed costs would fall by about a quarter, the team already works from home two days a week and mostly asked for more, the work is delivered digitally, and the biggest clients are comfortable with video check-ins.

premortem: Most new client projects over the last year came through walk-in meetings, referrals from the building's neighbours or in-person pitches at the studio, and without a place to meet, the pipeline slowly dries up without anyone noticing at first.
Junior designers, who were learning by sitting near seniors, lose mentoring and feedback; quality of work drops, two juniors leave within a year, and the senior staff become overloaded with review.

The survey showed a preference for remote days, but a few key people have home setups unsuitable for focused work or live in small flats, and their output falls; they quietly look for jobs with offices.

The home-working arrangement works legally and tax-wise only in the current setup; fully remote staff in other regions or countries trigger payroll, equipment and insurance obligations that erase much of the cost savings.

Two large clients that were fine with video check-ins actually value the studio visits for workshops and sign-offs; when the studio has no space they shift part of their work to an agency with premises.

beliefs.belief: Going remote cuts fixed costs by about a quarter.
beliefs.rests_on: The studio's own calculation of lease and office costs.
beliefs.how_wrong: It may leave out costs that appear after the move, such as co-working or meeting rooms, home-office stipends, software, equipment and insurance.

beliefs.belief: Staff want and can do effective work fully remote.
beliefs.rests_on: A team survey where most asked for more remote days.
beliefs.how_wrong: Asking for more remote days is not the same as wanting to be fully remote; the survey may not reflect quieter members or home conditions.

beliefs.belief: Team quality and collaboration will hold up without a shared office.
beliefs.rests_on: The experience of two remote days a week.
beliefs.how_wrong: Two days at home with three days together is a different situation from no shared days; the hybrid pattern was never tested as fully remote.

beliefs.belief: Biggest clients are fine with video calls for regular check-ins.
beliefs.rests_on: The team's impression from client conversations.
beliefs.how_wrong: It is an impression of the people managing accounts, and clients may not say they would prefer meeting in person; key kick-offs and sign-offs may differ from regular check-ins.

beliefs.belief: New client wins come from sources that do not depend on the office.
beliefs.rests_on: Assumption that the work is delivered digitally and the pitch can be remote.
beliefs.how_wrong: The studio's history of how recent projects were won has not been analyzed; some may have come through in-person events or local relationships.

beliefs.belief: The team can hire and train new people effectively remotely.
beliefs.rests_on: General experience and an assumption that talent is available.
beliefs.how_wrong: Past hiring happened with an office; onboarding juniors remotely was never tested, and candidates may prefer studios with offices.

beliefs.belief: The decision can be reversed if remote does not work.
beliefs.rests_on: The assumption that a space can be rented later.
beliefs.how_wrong: Finding a comparable space later may be costlier or slower, and key staff who leave in the meantime are not easily replaced.
